summary: This is a JUnit test that creates a Thermostat set to 60 degrees and checks that its status comes back as "Heating". It is the automated version of the by-hand check from the previous exercise: instead of you reading the output, JUnit compares it for you.

lines.text: This brings in the @Test annotation from JUnit 5, which is how you mark a method as a test that the test runner should execute.
A static import lets you write assertEquals(...) directly instead of Assertions.assertEquals(...), which keeps the test body short and readable.
Test classes conventionally take the name of the class under test with "Test" appended, so ThermostatTest holds the tests for Thermostat.
This annotation tells JUnit that the method below is a test case to run and report on.
A test method name should read like a sentence describing the expected behavior, so a failure report tells you exactly what broke.
This sets up the scenario under test by building a thermostat at 60 degrees, which is below the heating threshold.
The assertion states what should be true: the expected value comes first, the actual result second. If they differ, JUnit fails the test and shows both values.
